summary: Defines IPComp, a way to compress the payload of IP datagrams before they are sent. Compression helps most when encryption would otherwise make the data incompressible, because the data can be squeezed first and then protected. It is a proposed standard, replaced by RFC 3173.

eli5.summary: Imagine squeezing air out of a sleeping bag before you pack it. IPComp shrinks the data in each packet so it takes less room on the road.

questions: how does ip payload compression work
when should compression happen before encryption
what is a compression parameter index
subtitle: Compressing IP packet payloads to reduce bandwidth usage.

tldr.problem: IP datagrams consume bandwidth, and lower-layer compression cannot help when data is encrypted; networks need a way to squeeze payloads before transmission.
tldr.mechanism: IPComp compresses each IP datagram's payload independently before sending, inserting a 4-byte header with a compression algorithm identifier. If compression makes the packet larger, it is sent uncompressed instead. Each datagram is treated separately so packets can arrive out of order.
tldr.outcome: Networks with sufficient CPU resources can save bandwidth on slow or congested links, especially when encryption is applied (compress first, then encrypt). The protocol is meant to be negotiated through IPSec's ISAKMP or manual configuration.

today: RFC 2393 is a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 3173, which provides an updated IP payload compression specification.

sections.title: Motivation and Design
sections.content:
IP datagrams travel over physical links with finite bandwidth. Some applications or network conditions benefit from reducing packet size. Compression at the PPP layer (RFC 1962) can help, but only if the data is not encrypted.

When encryption is applied to data (for security), the encrypted output is random and does not compress well. However, if compression happens before encryption, the original data is squeezed, then the compressed data is encrypted. This order is essential: encryption destroys compressibility. IPComp allows hosts or gateways with sufficient CPU capacity to compress IP datagram payloads, provided the link is slow or congested enough that compression's CPU cost is justified by bandwidth savings.

The protocol is stateless: each datagram is compressed independently without tracking previous packets. This allows datagrams to arrive out of order or not at all without breaking the compression state.
sections.eli5: Compressing data before encrypting it lets you squeeze information first, then protect it. This only works if you do it in the right order.

sections.title: Compression and Decompression
sections.content:
Compression processing has two phases: outbound datagrams are compressed, and inbound datagrams are decompressed. The process MUST be lossless, ensuring the datagram is identical after compression and decompression. Inbound processing MUST support both compressed and non-compressed datagrams, because IPComp is optional; a sender may choose not to compress.

Compression happens before any IPSec processing (encryption or authentication) and before IP fragmentation. For IPv6, compression must happen before hop-by-hop options or routing headers, since those headers carry information that every hop along the path must examine. Decompression happens after reassembly and after all security processing (authentication and decryption).

The compression algorithm is applied to the upper-layer protocol payload. In IPv4, the entire ULP (upper layer protocol) payload is compressed. In IPv6, compression starts at the first IP header option that does not carry path information and continues through the ULP payload.
sections.eli5: The compressed data must be perfect: no information lost, no tiny errors. Each packet is its own isolated job, so one broken packet does not break the next one.

sections.title: The IPComp Header and IP Modifications
sections.content:
A 4-octet IPComp header is inserted immediately before the compressed payload. The header contains three fields:

  • Next Header (1 octet): Stores the IPv4 Protocol field or IPv6 Next Header field from the original IP header, so the receiving end knows what protocol came after the compression.
  • Flags (1 octet): Reserved for future use; currently must be zero and are ignored on reception.
  • Compression Parameter Index, or CPI (2 octets): Identifies the compression algorithm. Values 0-63 are well-known algorithms requiring no negotiation and are used for manual setup. Values 64-255 are reserved for future use. Values 256-61439 are negotiated between two nodes. Values 61440-65535 are for private use. The CPI, combined with the destination IP address, uniquely identifies the compression algorithm and its parameters.

In IPv4, the IP header's Protocol field is set to 108 (IPComp), and the Total Length is updated to reflect the compressed size. In IPv6, the Next Header field is set to 108, and the Payload Length is updated. All other IP header fields remain unchanged.
sections.eli5: The 4-byte label on the compressed data says what algorithm was used, what protocol is inside, and whether more data is coming after decompression.

sections.title: Non-Expansion Policy and Negotiation
sections.content:
Non-Expansion Policy: If the total size of the compressed payload plus the 4-byte IPComp header is larger than the original payload, the datagram MUST be sent uncompressed with no IPComp header. This prevents compression from wasting bandwidth and CPU. Small datagrams are likely to expand when compressed, so implementers should define a threshold below which compression is not attempted. An adaptive algorithm should also be implemented: if several consecutive datagrams fail to compress, the sender should skip compression for a number of subsequent datagrams and retry later. Once a datagram compresses successfully, normal compression resumes.

IPComp Association (IPCA): To use IPComp between two nodes, an IPComp Association must be established, containing the CPI, the mode (node-to-node or per-ULP-session), the compression algorithm, and any required parameters. The association can be negotiated dynamically via ISAKMP (Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol) when IPSec is present, or through manual configuration. Each direction can use a different algorithm, and one direction may be compressed while the other is not. The default is no compression.
sections.eli5: Don't compress if it makes the packet bigger. Agree with the other end on what algorithm to use, and be ready to turn compression on and off depending on whether it is actually helping.

sections.title: Security Impact
sections.content:
When IPComp is used with IPSec, compression does not degrade the underlying security functionality; encryption still protects the data and authentication still covers it. When IPComp is used alone (without IPSec), it potentially reduces security. A filtering router looking at IP header fields cannot see the original protocol number or transport layer ports inside a compressed datagram, because the IPComp header hides them. The original protocol field value is stored in the IPComp header, not in the normal position. This makes border router filtering problematic unless the router shares the IPComp Association with the sender and receiver.

Environments where all packets must be filtered or accounted for need a mechanism for the receiving node to securely communicate the IPComp Association to the border router, enabling stateful filtering even with compression.
sections.eli5: Compression hides the details of what is inside the packet, so border routers cannot see what protocol or port is inside. If you compress without encryption, security systems that filter packets by their contents get confused.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Original IPv4 Protocol or IPv6 Next Header field.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Reserved; must be zero and ignored on reception.

fields.name: Compression Parameter Index
fields.desc: Identifies the compression algorithm (0-63 well-known, 64-255 reserved, 256-61439 negotiated, 61440-65535 private).
